You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)

through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# Chroma - A General Purpose Syntax Highlighter

Chroma is a syntax highlighting library and command-line tool that takes source code and other structured text and converts it into syntax highlighted HTML, ANSI-coloured text, and other formats.

## Supported Languages

## Try it

Try out various languages and styles on the [Chroma Playground](https://swapoff.org/chroma/playground/).

## Command-line Interface

A command-line interface to Chroma is included.

Binaries are available to install from [the releases page](https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma/releases).

### Usage with `less`

The CLI can be used as a preprocessor to colorise output of `less(1)`,
see documentation for the `LESSOPEN` environment variable.

The `--fail` flag can be used to suppress output and return with exit status
1 to facilitate falling back to some other preprocessor in case chroma
does not resolve a specific lexer to use for the given file. For example:

```shell
export LESSOPEN='| p() { chroma --fail "$1" || cat "$1"; }; p "%s"'
```

Replace `cat` with your favourite fallback preprocessor.

When invoked as `.lessfilter`, the `--fail` flag is automatically turned
on under the hood for easy integration with [lesspipe shipping with
Debian and derivatives](https://manpages.debian.org/lesspipe#USER_DEFINED_FILTERS);
for that setup the `chroma` executable can be just symlinked to `~/.lessfilter`.

## Projects using Chroma

* [`moor`](https://github.com/walles/moor) is a full-blown pager that colorizes
  its input using Chroma
* [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/) is a static site generator that [uses Chroma for syntax
  highlighting code examples](https://gohugo.io/content-management/syntax-highlighting/)

## Try it

Try out various languages and styles on the [Chroma Playground](https://swapoff.org/chroma/playground/).

## Command-line Interface

A command-line interface to Chroma is included.

Binaries are available to install from [the releases page](https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma/releases).

### Usage with `less`

The CLI can be used as a preprocessor to colorise output of `less(1)`,
see documentation for the `LESSOPEN` environment variable.

The `--fail` flag can be used to suppress output and return with exit status
1 to facilitate falling back to some other preprocessor in case chroma
does not resolve a specific lexer to use for the given file. For example:

```shell
export LESSOPEN='| p() { chroma --fail "$1" || cat "$1"; }; p "%s"'
```

Replace `cat` with your favourite fallback preprocessor.

When invoked as `.lessfilter`, the `--fail` flag is automatically turned
on under the hood for easy integration with [lesspipe shipping with
Debian and derivatives](https://manpages.debian.org/lesspipe#USER_DEFINED_FILTERS);
for that setup the `chroma` executable can be just symlinked to `~/.lessfilter`.

## Projects using Chroma

* [`moor`](https://github.com/walles/moor) is a full-blown pager that colorizes
  its input using Chroma
* [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/) is a static site generator that [uses Chroma for syntax
  highlighting code examples](https://gohugo.io/content-management/syntax-highlighting/)

# The real complexity is the lexer definitions

# 3. Chroma shows "()" as one Punctuation token
# 4. Chroma: LiteralString for the import, Pygments: Literal.String
# 5. Pygments doesn't merge NameOther.Println as function

# The pattern of merging adjacent same-type tokens is consistent in chroma
# And chroma treats Text.Whitespace differently from Python (shows as TextWhitespace vs Text)

# But for Go, chroma shows "TextWhitespace"!
# This is because the lexers use different token types:
# - Python lexer emits Text.Whitespace -> chroma maps to "TextWhitespace" 
# - But we saw Python showed "Text"... let me check again

echo 'x = 1
y = 2' | ./executable -l python -f json -s monokai 2>&1

# Better approach: Look at the trace output differently.
# Group rules (like "(import)((?:\s|\\\s)+)") emit tokens for each group.
# Single-group rules emit one token.

# For Python, the trace shows rule 12 for "import " and the token is "KeywordNamespace" for "import"
# This is a multi-group rule where group 1 is Keyword and group 2 is Text.

import subprocess
import json
import re

code = 'import sys\nx = 1\ny = "hello"\n'

trace_proc = subprocess.run(
    ['./executable', '-l', 'python', '-s', 'monokai', '--trace', '-f', 'tokens'],
    input=code, capture_output=True, text=True
)

trace_data = []
for line in trace_proc.stderr.split('\n'):
    try:
        trace_data.append(json.loads(line))
    except:
        pass

token_data = []
for line in trace_proc.stdout.split('\n'):
    m = re.match(r'&Token\{(\w+),\s+"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"\}', line)
    if m:
        val = m.group(2).replace('\\"', '"').replace('\\n', '\n').replace('\\t', '\t')
        token_data.append({'type': m.group(1), 'value': val})

print("Trace:")
for t in trace_data:

print("\nTokens:")
for t in token_data:
    print(f"  {t['type']}: {t['value']!r}")

import subprocess
import json
import re

def test_rule(lang, code, expected_trace_pattern, binary='./executable'):
    """Test a specific piece of code and see what tokens are produced"""
    proc = subprocess.run(
        [binary, '-l', lang, '-s', 'monokai', '--trace', '-f', 'tokens'],
        input=code + '\n', capture_output=True, text=True
    )
    
    trace_data = []
    for line in proc.stderr.split('\n'):
        try:
            trace_data.append(json.loads(line))
        except:
            pass
    
    token_data = []
    for line in proc.stdout.split('\n'):
        m = re.match(r'&Token\{(\w+),\s+"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"\}', line)
        if m:
            token_data.append(m.group(1))
    
    return trace_data, token_data

# Test individual Python rules:
tests = [
    ('1', 'LiteralNumberInteger'),
    ('1.5', 'LiteralNumberFloat'),
    ('0xFF', 'LiteralNumberHex'),
    ('0o77', 'LiteralNumberOct'),
    ('0b101', 'LiteralNumberBin'),
    ('"hello"', 'LiteralStringDouble'),
    ("'hello'", 'LiteralStringSingle'),
    ('# comment', 'CommentSingle'),
    ('True', 'KeywordConstant'),
    ('None', 'KeywordConstant'),
    ('False', 'KeywordConstant'),
    ('print', 'NameBuiltin'),
    ('int', 'NameBuiltin'),
    ('x', 'Name'),
    (' ', 'Text'),
    ('=', 'Operator'),
    ('and', 'OperatorWord'),
    ('not', 'OperatorWord'),
    ('(', 'Punctuation'),
    (':=', 'Operator'),
    ('import os', '...'),
    ('from os import path', '...'),
    ('def foo():', '...'),
    ('class Bar:', '...'),
    ('if True:', '...'),
]

for code, expected in tests:
    trace, tokens = test_rule('python', code)
    first_trace = trace[0] if trace else None
    first_token = tokens[0] if tokens else None
    match = '✓' if first_token == expected or expected == '...' else '✗'
    print(f"{match} Code: {code!r:20s} Rule:{first_trace['rule'] if first_trace else 'N/A':4} Token:{first_token!r:25s} Expected:{expected!r}")

        m = re.match(r'&Token\{(\w+),\s+"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"\}', line)

            token_data.append(m.group(1))

# - Rule 4: "" (empty pattern) matches nothing, pops "import" state

# CRITICAL PROBLEM: Go's RE2 doesn't support lookbehind!
# But chroma uses lookbehind patterns like:
# - (?<!\.)(word...) for Python builtins
# - (?<!\.)(\w+) for various patterns

# I need to handle lookbehind specially.
# Options:
# 1. Use a different regex library that supports lookbehind
# 2. Simulate lookbehind by checking the character before the match
# 3. Use a preprocessing step to convert lookbehind patterns

# Let me check if there's a Go regex library with lookbehind support:
# regexp/syntax doesn't support it
# github.com/dlclark/regexp2 supports PCRE with lookbehind
# But I can't download it from the internet

# Let me check what lookbehind patterns are used in the Python lexer:
echo '(?<!\.)(print)\n' | ./executable -l python -s monokai --trace 2>&1 | head -3

# For Python, rule 41 uses: (?<!\.)(...builtin names...) 
# This means "builtin name NOT preceded by a dot"
# e.g., "print" is builtin but ".print" is not

# The workaround: Instead of lookbehind, I can check if the previous character
# was a dot after the match and skip if so.
# But this is complex to implement.

# Alternative: Use a post-processing step:
# If the pattern uses lookbehind, use a different strategy:
# 1. First try to match WITHOUT the lookbehind
# 2. Then check if the lookbehind condition is satisfied
# 3. If not, skip this rule

# Actually, let me look at how many patterns use lookbehind:
python3 << 'PYEOF'
import subprocess, json, re

proc = subprocess.run(
    ['./executable', '-l', 'python', '-s', 'monokai', '--trace', '-f', 'tokens'],
    input='''
print(x)
int(y)
x.print(z)
''', capture_output=True, text=True
)

trace_data = []
for line in proc.stderr.split('\n'):
    try:
        trace_data.append(json.loads(line))
    except:
        pass

lookbehind_patterns = set()
for t in trace_data:
    if '(?<!' in t.get('pattern', ''):
        lookbehind_patterns.add(t['pattern'][:50])
        
print("Lookbehind patterns:", lookbehind_patterns)

for line in proc.stdout.split('\n'):
    m = re.match(r'&Token\{(\w+),\s+"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"\}', line)
    if m:
        print(f"  {m.group(1)}: {m.group(2)!r}")

# There are many mismatches. The terminal8 color conversion is complex.
# Let me just create a lookup table directly from the test data:

python3 << 'ENDSCRIPT'
import re

with open('/tmp/cube_mapping.txt') as f:
    lines = f.readlines()

# Build lookup table: (r_idx, g_idx, b_idx) -> (bold, ansi_code)
table = {}
for line in lines:
    m = re.match(r'\s*\((\d),(\d),(\d)\) (#\w+) -> 8=\[(.+?)\] 256=(38;5;(\d+))', line)
    if m:
        r_idx = int(m.group(1))
        g_idx = int(m.group(2))
        b_idx = int(m.group(3))
        ansi8 = [x.strip("'").strip() for x in m.group(5).replace("'", "").split(', ')]
        idx256 = int(m.group(7))
        
        if len(ansi8) >= 2 and ansi8[0] == '1':
            bold = True
            color = int(ansi8[1])
        else:
            bold = False
            color = int(ansi8[0])
        
        # key: 256-color index (16+36*r+6*g+b)
        key = 16 + 36*r_idx + 6*g_idx + b_idx
        assert key == idx256, f"{key} != {idx256}"
        table[key] = (bold, color)

print(f"Lookup table has {len(table)} entries")

# Generate Go code for the lookup table
print("\n// 256-to-8 color lookup table")
print("var cube256to8 = [216]int{")
for i in range(216):
    key = i + 16
    if key in table:
        bold, color = table[key]
        ansi_val = (1 if bold else 0) * 100 + color
        print(f"    {ansi_val}, // {i}: bold={bold} color={color}")
    else:
        print(f"    0, // {i}: missing!")
print("}")
ENDSCRIPT

# This means: bold+white + reset + newline
# The COLOR is applied but the value "\n" comes AFTER the reset!

# Mine does: \e[1m\e[37m\n\e[0m
# This means: bold+white + newline + reset

# So the original applies colors but puts the VALUE before the reset...
# Actually looking at this more carefully:
# Original: \e[1m\e[37m \e[0m is for the EMPTY value "" after the \n
# No wait... the token has value "\n"

# Original: \e[33m1\e[0m \e[1m\e[37m \e[0m \n
# The \n comes AFTER all the ANSI sequences!
# This means the last token (Text "\n") outputs: color + "" + reset + "\n"???
# No, that doesn't make sense either.

# Let me look again:
# Original bytes at end: ...1 033[0m 033[1m 033[37m 033[0m \n
# Pattern: 1 + RESET + BOLD + WHITE + RESET + NEWLINE
# 
# So the last token "\n" outputs: BOLD+WHITE + RESET (but NOT the \n)
# Then the \n is output AFTER?
# 
# Wait, that can't be right. Let me count the tokens:
# x " " = " " 1 "\n" -> that's 6 tokens
# But the output shows: color(x) color(" ") color(=) color(" ") color(1) color("") \n
# So the "\n" token doesn't emit its value in the escape-colored form!

# Actually I think I understand now:
# The LAST token with value "\n" - chroma splits the value at the last newline
# and outputs the escaped part WITHOUT the newline, then outputs the newline separately

# OR: The terminal formatter strips trailing newlines from the last token

# Let me look more carefully:
# Token: Text "\n" 
# Original output: \e[1m\e[37m\e[0m\n
# This is: bold+white for "" (empty string) + reset + \n
# So the token value "\n" was output as "" + "\n", where the "" gets the color and "\n" doesn't?

# Actually I think what's happening:
# The terminal formatter splits each token value at newlines
# For the Text "\n" token:
# - Before \n: "" (empty, gets colored but invisible)
# - The \n itself: output without color
# This is a common pattern in terminal formatters!

# My fix: Split token values at newlines for the terminal formatter:

echo "Need to split token values at newlines for terminal output"
